utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Cermak Defence -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not a Cermak Defence but since you're on your feet, I take it that there's something out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask a question after the Court finishes with the preliminaries, just a procedural question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you consider to be the preliminaries. We have dealt with it, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was waiting for the Court to see if we were going call the next witness. We just on behalf of the Gotovina Defence wanted to just ask that the Court consider the lineup of cross-examination with respect to the next witness. We understand that there will be a process here and the witness will be giving his evidence in direct. There are -- there are likely to be based on the proofing note we got, changes to one of his statements. That will and has impacted our time estimate that we originally gave the Chamber. The Court will recall that we originally asked for three sessions of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will now be less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will now be less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, presumably, yes. But that was based on our -- what we believed our 90(H) obligation to be, with respect to certain portions of the statement. I have had a conversation with the Prosecution. I suspect in their cross-examination they will be challenging the changes to the statement which then again depending on what happens in their cross-examination could lead to a need for an extensive redirect -- a recross, I should say, by the Gotovina Defence depending on what happens in their cross. So in terms of the efficiency of how we're going to do this, I just wanted to put out there to the Chamber that it may be more efficient if the Prosecution in this one instance goes first with cross-examination so that we know exactly what it is we're supposed to be cross-examining on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what is the position of the Prosecution in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we see no reason to change the normal order of cross-examination, and I don't think it would increase the efficiency. If Mr. Misetic wants to deal with the statement as it stands, he is free to do that; if he wants to address any changes, he is free to do that. There's a good reason, Your Honour, that the Prosecution goes last, and I don't see any reason to change that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, just on the last point, Your Honour, we've actually looked into it, and I don't know that's in the rules that the Prosecution gets to go last. It's just sort of the practice that has been accepted, and there's been no objection to it, but I don't think there is any rule that actually lays that out in that fashion. And in this particular case let me also add that it actually does affect how we would cross-examine. Obviously I'm not going to cross-examine a witness on matters that the witness, on direct examination, says he didn't say and doesn't stand by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are several elements in the question and the answer. First, Ms. Gustafson, I noticed that you didn't say we object to it, but that you said that there are no good reasons for changing it. Second is that you addressed two matters. The first is the efficiency and then you continued to say that the Gotovina Defence, of course, could cross-examine as they wish. I think no one disputes that right, but whether that that's efficient or not, of course, is something still to be considered. And finally you said there were good reasons why we have adopted this practice. Of course, the issue is whether those good reasons, if spelled out, would lead to the conclusion that, under the present circumstances, we should not proceed as suggested. I'm not giving any opinion at this moment yet, but I just noticed that there are a few loose ends still in the -- what was submitted to the Chamber. Both -- also from Mr. Misetic, of course, we do not know exactly what he has on his mind. I don't know what he wants to cross-examine the witness on, so, therefore, quite many loose ends.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I should have been more clear. I think the good reasons and the efficiency are one in the same in the sense that many times the other cross-examinations -- the cross-examinations of the other Defence teams need to be addressed by the Prosecution in cross-examination, so it is efficient and makes sense that the Prosecution goes last. I don't see any reason that that should change in that case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see how matters develop. Mr. Kay, are you ready to call your next witness, who I understand is Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I call Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher. Mr. Kay, could I draw your attention already to the following. There is a suggestion that a document, which is a minutes of the government session to be added to the 65 ter list, and I take it that you want to do that, in order to tender that document. Now, in view of what happened yesterday, would you please consider whether D1634 would do as good as adding a document to the 65 ter list and then tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning -- good morning, Mr. Pasic. You're looking in a direction where the speaker is not to be found. I'm the one who speaks at this moment, Mr. Pasic, yes. Mr. Pasic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Please be seated. Mr. Pasic, you will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at a document, first of all, which is a record of the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution in 2001 and 2002. I see you've got some papers in front of you there, and looking at them, they seem to be the hard copies of what we're going to look at on a computer screen. On the right-hand side, you will see in a moment a document come up, 2D00-722. If you just put those other papers away in front of you, just put them in the folder, and if you need to refer to them, you can do, and ask -- ask the Court's permission. Now, what you will see on the screen coming up in a moment is a statement in two languages. On the right-hand side, is your own language, but on the left-hand side is a statement in the English language and is a record of that interview in 2001 and 2002. And can you see your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I can. It's on the left side in the English language copy, but I cannot see it in the Croatian copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's all right. It's the English document that was signed. I'm going to ask to you look at a series of these documents and just identify them for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can just turn to the last page of the -- second-to-last page of the English document, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, can you see your signature there at the end of this statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I can't see my signature in the Croatian version; only on the English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's the English copy that we're looking at for these purposes. And do you confirm that you signed this document that the Office of the Prosecution produced with you on the 3rd of March, 2002?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And your signature is on the bottom of each page in between. The next document I want to look at is 2D00-712. This is a document, when it comes on the screen, which is a record of an interview you gave to the Defence, first in the year 2007, then in the year 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we can look at the Croatian version, please, this time down at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you confirm your signature on the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the last page, page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the last page of that record of the interview you gave with the Defence on the 23rd of April, 2009, when it was signed. And do you identify there your signature on the last page?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your signature is also on the pages in between, and I'm going to ask you some questions now. The statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution, did you read that statement and make some corrections to that document in the statement that you gave to the Defence and signed in 2009?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you signed this statement for the Defence, did you read through your Defence statement to ensure that that content was true and correct to the knowledge of your -- best knowledge of your belief?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document I want you to look at is document 2D00-763. And you can see a document here, which is headed: Supplemental Information Sheet and contains corrections to that statement you originally gave to the Office of the Prosecution that you wanted made on the 2nd of September, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the document in e-court isn't signed. There -- this has been signed and uploaded into the system, so we're looking at a document that is to be perfected. It was signed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay. Unless there is any reason to doubt, and I see no reason whatsoever, that it would be the same document but now signed that we could proceed for the time being on the basis of what we see on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The signed document will be attached to this, I'm told, within the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you can just look at that document there, Mr. Pasic, in your own language and look at the matters raised within that supplemental information sheet. Do you confirm that these were corrections that you gave to the Defence concerning that statement to the OTP when we met on the 2nd of September, 2009?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow an explanation --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to look at page 2 of this before you say anything, just to confirm the information on page 2. If you look at page 2 on your screen, do you confirm there those matters that you raised with the Defence, and you wanted to make corrections to the statement of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is everything that you said within this supplemental information sheet, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you confirm that you have read through this supplemental information sheet and that you signed this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you now to look at a second supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can 2D00-764 be placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you see there on the right-hand side in your own language a further supplemental information sheet?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you confirm that on the 6th of October, when you met me to discuss and confirm your statements, that you requested further corrections be made to your statement to the Office of the Prosecution, which was signed on the 3rd of March, 2002?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, there is a signed version of this because it had to be typed up overnight, signed yesterday, which has been uploaded into e-court and we await its connection with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you said it had to be typed up, does that mean that the witness has not seen the final result?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He has seen it, Your Honour. JUDE ORIE: He has.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just about to ask him that. I was just informing Your Honour that we were in the same procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you look at that page of the document, Mr. Pasic, and confirm that you have read this document and signed a statement for that document yesterday? If you look at the first page, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I believe you have copies with you in court today in the paper form; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we just look at page 2, can you confirm when you signed this document yesterday that you read this page?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3, can you confirm that when you signed this document yesterday that you read this page?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 4. Can you confirm, when page 4 is on the screen, that you have read this and signed this document yesterday? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And page 5, can you confirm that you read this in your own language and signed it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And page 6, I believe, in the Croatian version as well, do you confirm you read that and signed that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge and belief, is the information contained within this second supplement, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, looking at the information within these four documents, taking into account the corrections made in documents that were produced after the Prosecution statement, if you were to be asked these questions again in court today, would you give the answers as corrected within these statements and provide the same information to the Court?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: With the corrections, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the 92 ter procedure, and I ask that the four documents be made exhibits. Your Honour, the Court will recollect that one of these had been produced earlier in the proceedings and was marked for identification. That's the document which was the original Prosecution statement, which had been marked for identification as D1307. I believe it was eventually vacated from the list, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to check that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps new numbers should be given to all four in sequence, might be a more satisfactory way of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, Mr. Registrar will certainly, at this moment verify whether D1307 was vacated. I would have one question for you. Do you consider the B/C/S or Croatian cover page of the 2001/2002 statement to be a full translation of the original English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All can I say is, Your Honour, this will have come off the document system. I don't have a copy of that just in -- in front of me. The original statement is the English statement and the other document has been translated later into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I might be able to assist, Your Honour. The cover page actually extends onto the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But even including the second page, do you consider this to be a full translation of the English original? I hope you will be forgive me for being a bit suspicious. When looking at the layout, I see that there are some difference. First of all, and that might not be of great importance, I do not see in the B/C/S version any telephone numbers or addresses, which I find in the English original. But it seems to me - but please correct me when I'm wrong - when I'm looking at the languages, I see three entries in the original, the first one is languages spoken. There it says, Croatian. And languages written, if different from spoken, where, in the original, says that that's Croatian, but in the translation it seems that no answer to that question is given at all. Now, it could well be that the whole of the document is well translated, but, apparently, someone, apart from being what I consider, at this moment, to be most likely sloppy by just leaving out a part of the information, some, perhaps by mistake, that is, the written language different from spoken, to be Croatian. Of course, it's not different; it's the same. But that's, I would say, the sloppiness of the one who drafted the document. But apparently for one reason or another the interpreter also considered it appropriate to leave out addresses, telephones numbers. Of course, I do not know what elsewhere in this document the translator considered to be appropriate to leave out or ... I see that it's not what I expect, and I'm looking both at you, Mr. Kay, and Ms. Gustafson, you intervened as well. What I expect from a translation, that it literally in every respects reflects what the original says. And that's apparently not the case with this cover page. Unless would you disagree with me. And therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I totally agree, otherwise -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... Yes, and then of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- we're not able to comprehend. JUDE ORIE: It could just that it's just the cover page, and it's perhaps even very likely, but nevertheless, it seems that someone considered that it was right to not do what I would expect that person to do, is that just to reflect in the other language what the original says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For this reason, I would like to draw the attention of the parties to it, that it should be carefully checked whether similar problems arise elsewhere in the document, which, of course, I cannot verify. The only way for me to look this is cover pages that still -- I can decipher those, but not the text itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The second supplemental information sheet in paragraph 16 deals with an issue of test that was in the English original that is not in the Croatian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's a point -- made there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm encouraging and more or less insisting on great precision in this respect, because otherwise we end up in all kind of problems, where the problems -- the real problems we have are big enough not to be further -- we're not in need of any additional problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, for the time being, Mr. Kay, and I would like to have this verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, shall we deal with the exhibit numbering through the Registry at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take that the Registrar has by now verified D1307. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, D1307 was marked for identification on 13th February 2009 and subsequently vacated on 3rd March 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please assign numbers to the documents Mr. Kay has uploaded and put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 2D00-722 becomes Exhibit D1706; 65 ter number 2D00-712 becomes Exhibit D1707; 65 ter number 2D00-763 becomes Exhibit D1708; and 65 ter number 2D00-764 becomes Exhibit D1709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we are talking about the statement given to the Prosecution, statement given to the Defence, first and second additional information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D706, D707 -- no D1706, D1707, D1708, and D1709 are admitted into evidence. And the Chamber expects the parties to carefully review original and translation, specifically in relation to the statement given to the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Within the statements, there are certain documents referred to that I would seek to make exhibits. The first one concerns 2D00-713, which is in the exhibit D1706.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 3, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if you could just briefly say -- in your motion you -- you refer to a description of the document. I'm -- just numbers, you're talking to a letter to Serbs, letter to Franjo Tudjman. Which one --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This one is PP1. Which Your Honour will see in paragraph 3 of page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is what? I could, of course, check, but I would rather talk --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was missing what Your Honour was saying there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because in your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In Mr. Pasic's letter to the Serbian citizens in Knin before the start of the Geneva negotiations, and that would refer an OTP statement which we felt should therefore be seen by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May that be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1710.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Ms. Gustafson, I take it. Then D1710 is admitted into evidence. Next one, letter to Franjo Tudjman, I take it, 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Page 3, paragraph 6, Your Honour. It's marked PP2. And it's 2D00-714, referred to in exhibit 1706. We ask that that be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Gustafson, whenever you say no objection, I take that implicitly Mr. Kay has asked for adding it to the 65 ter list and that no objection extends to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1711.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Letter of protest concerning appearance of Split county chief of 6th of August, Mr. Kay, I see as next one in your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 2D00715, may we add this to the 65 ter list, Your Honour, and my apologies for not following my script and requesting permission previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection to that, or to it being made an exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1712 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kay, the last one in your motion are the minutes I earlier referred to, and I would really like to avoid similar events that happened yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, what this is, is an extra part of the document that's -- that's not reflected in the exhibit D1634 which was connected to it. And it's an annex to it, and that is the part that we were essentially adding to it, but we had an entire document. We haven't taken it apart, so what the Court will have is a conjoined document with both parts together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, should we make it an exhibit, I think it might be preferable to have the full document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least, and that's the difference with yesterday, we know what we are doing, and that's -- Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're talking about document here 2D00-716.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1713.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1713 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For references purposes, that's page 4, paragraph 14 that is referred to. The next document, Your Honour ... Your Honour, those are the documents that we need to tender and make exhibits, and I will now give a short summary of the nature of -- of Mr. Pasic's evidence, with the court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic was the government commissioner, also called the trustee, for Knin. He took -- took on that position from 1992 and was appointed on the 6th of January of that year. He was the government's representative dealing with issues prior to the liberation of the occupied territories. And upon the liberation of Knin and the occupied territories, he went to Knin to take on his civil duties. He arrived in Knin and soon connected with General Cermak, and the two of them set about tasks for the normalization of life in Knin. His evidence refers to the fact that General Cermak helped him do his work and, as he understood it, that was General Cermak's job in Knin, which was to help the civilian authorities to organise the return of people to Knin and create normal conditions of life in Knin. His evidence refers to the nature of the work they undertook, dealing with the public services, establishing a bus line, dealing with essential matters that were needed to both feed and look after the people who had come to the area, as well as who were working in the area. And, in those circumstances, him and Mr. Cermak worked together, and Mr. Cermak's position as the garrison commander, helped Mr. Pasic in the performance of his tasks. Your Honour, that is a brief summary of the nature of the witness's evidence, and in view of the fact that he has made his statements, I have no further questions to ask of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- pointed out to me that there was one other document on the OTP statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was just asking about the fifth document which is 65 ter 3481, which was mentioned in the Appendix B to your motion which was already on the 65 ter list, but what you indicated that would you tender that document as well. And that was a letter by Mr. Pasic to the police in Zadar and Knin, concerning the theft of grapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a -- it's a document from the Prosecution 65 ter list. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it was already on their list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. [Overlapping speakers]... Your Honour, that is found at page 5, paragraph 7, of his OTP statement, and I ask that that be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1714.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1714 is admitted into evidence. I take it, Mr. Kay, that it doesn't change your summary in any way. Now we are at a point of having to decide on the sequence of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to take a minute to consider the request by the Gotovina Defence. Now, that would be Prosecution first - that's at least your suggestion - but I haven't heard about any reasons for the Markac Defence. First of all, is there any need to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Markac Defence would have no questions on that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that problem doesn't arise. The Chamber will take a minute to consider the matter, how to proceed, and the parties are expected to remain stand by. --- Break taken at 9.56 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered your request, Mr. Misetic, to change the usual order of cross-examination. Your request is denied. At the same time, the Chamber adds to this, that the Chamber will be liberal - I wouldn't use the word generous - but if you would raise matters in re-cross, which were left out from your initial cross-examination, because at this moment have you no reasons, although you have already warned the Chamber that they might be very relevant and might take considerable time in re-cross if Ms. Gustafson deals with those matters and if she challenges portions of the original statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, we bothered you with all kind of procedural technicalities for quite a while. We hope that we can now further focus on your testimony. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you just as a preliminary matter just a few questions on some of the changes made to your 2002 statement. Could you explain to the Court why it is that you only made these changes upon your arrival to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: For a long time, I didn't read the statement that I had given to the OTP closely, and when I felt that the time of my travel to The Hague was moving close, once I was informed of the date when I should appear here, I understood the seriousness of the situation, and I analysed every paragraph thoroughly. It was then that I noticed that some things that I had said then were not correct, and that I couldn't give the solemn declaration of speaking the truth and the whole truth and nothing but the truth if I stand by those parts of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me show you a couple of documents first and then I would like to get back and ask you a few questions on this topic. But -- let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. President. If I could have 65 ter 1D2983 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, while this is coming up, do you believe that there was an official policy of the Croatian government to allow criminal activity, including burning, looting, and murder to take place in the territory of former Sector South after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to some comments attributed to you in 1996, and this is from a news organisation known as AIM, which I believe, Mr. President, is an NGO news letter. The article is titled: Deserted roads of Knin, it's dated the 5th of April, 1996. And there are some quotes from you. It talks about the fact that you had been replaced as the commissioner for the town of Knin and then appointed to the post of commissioner of the newly established municipalities of Kistanje, Ervenik, Orlic, and Civljane, and that's in the second paragraph. And then it says -- the next paragraph says: "To a question about recent quarrels with the local leaders of the Croat Democratic Community HDZ who had 'asked for his head' for months, Mr. Pasic answers that tensions were directed against him 'not as a man who just wishes to help, but as a man who was not a member of the rule party and a man of Serb nationality.'" And then this is the quote I want to ask you the question about: "When the last opportunity was given to those people in negotiations in Geneva, I was the one who addressed them and asked them to stay in their state, to finally see how tragic everything is that their self-proclaimed leaders brought them to, which resulted in the exodus they were pushed into. I wished those people to remain, and an I now [sic] advocate that these people be given the right to a normal life. Individual excesses do not reflect the stance of the official policy, Mr. Pasic ends his statement." Can you explain to the Court what you meant when you said that "individual excesses do not reflect the stance of the official policy"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of the security situation in the town of Knin, it was always possible for individual incidents to happen. The -- it depends on people who are prone to cause incidents. Some were probably based on ethnic rivalry or hatred, but those were individual incidents. I stand by my statement that this wasn't encouraged from the Croatian Government or authorities or any official institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph I want to ask you to clarify. You said -- you asked them to stay in their state to finally see how tragic everything is that their self-proclaimed leaders brought them to, which resulted in the exodus they were pushed into. Can you clarify what you meant when you said that they were pushed into an exodus. Who pushed them into an exodus?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: On that day, that was the 17th or 18th of August, when the first roadblocks were put up, when the Croatian independence was proclaimed among some -- in some quarters in the Serbian community, there was this negative attitude toward the Croatian state and the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just so we clarify, you say 17 of August, you're referring to 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You can continue your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: After that, unfortunately, in the territories mostly populated by Serbs, the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina was created which disgruntled the Croats. And that is why these negative attitudes or tensions were more pronounced than they should have been. I was appointed commissioner of the Croatian government. I must correct Mr. Kay, not on the 6th of January but on the 4th of January. And at that time I wasn't being discriminated against. I was -- I was a citizen of Croatia of Serb ethnicity. I was a member of the SDP party then, and I even said in a broadcast that I was a atheist which at the time was not a popular thing to say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last sentence the witness said. Could he please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last sentence; the interpreter didn't hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: As a citizen of Croatia of Serbian ethnicity, I was a member of the SDP and a atheist. Among the candidates for the post of commissioner, I was appointed. So there was no negative discrimination toward me as a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I stopped you because I want go back to the specific question, if can you recall. When you said that the Serbs had been pushed into an exodus, do you recall who or what pushed them into an exodus?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: The Serbs had, for a long time, be linked for the then Yugoslavia and the Yugoslav People's Army, and they couldn't accept the existence of an independent state of Croatia. I personally consider that their leaders who were there already pushed them into that exodus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Continuing on this exhibit, two paragraphs beneath that, you said -- you were asked: "To a question whether the Serbs are returning and how many of them have actually returned, Petar Pasic says that 'in the territory of the town of Knin 420 citizens of Serb nationality have remained and more than 300 have already returned. I am not at all in favour of the return of those who have committed crimes, nor those who have participated in demolition of democratic Croatia. By their arrival and mere appearance, they would create uneasiness among the Croats who have returned and they would disturb the good relations between the Croats and the Serbs.'" And if we go into the next paragraph: "This was, after all, the epicentre of the rebellion against the Croat state, and when the Serbs do return here, it is necessary to take great care who should be allowed to come, and in what way, says Mr. Pasic. What is being said now, what Babic and Mikelic have been doing lately, I think it is pure deception of those people again, because they have done it all the time, all four years. I think they probably expect some kind of humanitarian aid to use those people, or use it only for themselves, as they have done here." Now a few questions on this -- these passages. First, do you recall when you said, "... what Babic and Mikelic have been doing lately," what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, in this quote you say: "What is being said now, what Babic and Mikelic have been doing lately, I think it is pure deception of those people again." And you said this in April of 1996. Do you recall what it is that Babic and Mikelic were doing lately?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the information I have, there was a talk about the establishment of some provisional authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you reference in this passage that 300 Serbs had already returned. Do you remember where they had returned from?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: When I saw the documents they had upon them when they returned, I saw that most of their personal ID, including passports, were issued in Vukovar and Beli Manastir. And as those towns are close to Serbia, I supposed that they returned from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. As the commissioner in the town of Knin, can you tell us whether there were obstacles put in the place of these 300 people to come back?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any involvement in caring for or housing these people, once they had returned from Serbia or Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: We assisted in the cooperation with the Social Welfare Centre at Knin. We provided initially some financial assistance and, later on, we gave them also some clothes and shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As the commissioner in Knin, after Operation Storm and through March of 1996, did you feel that there were obstacles being put in the place -- in place to prevent people from coming back?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No. Not as far as I know. There weren't any obstacles for those who were willing to return, who had expressed the wish to return, to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Explain to us what you meant when you said "this was, after all, the epicentre of the rebellion against the Croat state. And when the Serbs do return here, it is necessary to take great care who should be allowed to come and in what way."

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Since the town of Knin had been settled by ethnic Croats from Banja Luka who had been expelled from there and also Croats from the surroundings of Knin, I considered that it wouldn't contribute to building up good relations as they had existed before, to include the ring leaders of the rebellion or those who had perpetrated crimes into the process of return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1715.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1715 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the reference to Babic and Mikelic in April of 1996, I asked you what you recalled of that, in terms of why you reference them. But let me now show you Exhibit D1610, and that will come up on your screen. And this is an article that appeared in the same news -- news organisation, one month prior to the interview that you gave. So this is 7th of March, 1996, and the article is titled: Mr. Mikelic leading the way. Mr. Mikelic, as you know, was one of the leaders of the Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S, please. I'm looking at the last two paragraphs on both pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Dr. Milan Babic who claims that he had not met Borislav Mikelic since the exodus of the Serbs from the Krajina and that he, therefore, knew nothing about the intentions of the committee, but what he was told by third parties, says as follows: "I am not in favour of individual solutions of the problem of return, because it would mean Croatisation of the Serb returnees, which would jeopardize collective rights of the refugees and blur the problem of the Serb people in exile. I am in favour of collective return, collective security, and collective rights of the Serbs which implies resolution of their political status. Because the Serbs from Krajina - Dr. Babic continues - have the political right to the territory of Krajina. If the committee of Borislav Mikelic approaches the problem of resolving the return of Serb refugees in this way, there will be no conflicts between us - Dr. Babic says - adding that the government of the Krajina operates in exile and that a special commission was established within it to deal with the issues of the status and rights of the refugees, cooperation with various organisations and institutions, so why not Mikelic too." Do you recall whether your comments a month later were directed at what Mr. Babic and Mr. Mikelic were -- I should say, Mr. Babic was talking about in terms of collective return as opposed to individual return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I have seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, Mr. Pasic, we saw in the exhibit that was just admitted where you said that individual excesses do not reflect the stance of the official policy. And you've said the same thing essentially in the proofing statement that you signed yesterday, that you did not believe that it was government policy to allow for criminal activity to take place. Your 2002 statement, however, has a passage where - and let me find it - this is page 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D1706, page 8. I believe it's page ... Yes, this is the second-to-last paragraph on the page in English. And let me ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it's page 14 of B/C/S, if that's what Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, counsel. It's page 14, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your 2002 statement, it's recorded as you having said: "I believe that the looting and destruction that took place was planned from above. It was anarchy in Knin, only the president could have stopped it." My question to you is: In 1996 you had said that -- and I understand that, obviously, sir, you that say that that is not accurate and you don't believe that, and that's what you said in your proofing statement. My question to you is: In 1996, you had said publicly you didn't believe it was official policy to condone such activity. You said the same thing now in 2009. Can you tell us how it is that that conclusion came up in 2002?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I think -- well, I don't think I said anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I did not have my eye on the clock, and this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is time for a break. We will have a break, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to continue by asking you some questions about some documents that have been already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D56 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, do you recall having meetings with a gentleman named Husein Al-Alfi, in the period after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a document which purports to record the results of Mr. Al-Alfi's meeting with you and Mr. Cermak on the 18th of August, 1995. And you'll see that -- in the first paragraph, Mr. Al-Alfi reports that: "This morning I had a meeting with ... Petar Pasic, the mayor of Knin." He also records who else was present at the meeting. If you look on your screen, I think you might be able to see the document. Do you recall this meeting where Mr. Djakovic and Mr. Vidovic were also present?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we turn to page 2, which is subparagraph (f). Mr. Al-Alfi says: "I brought to the attention of the mayor, the reports about continuing burning of villages and looting until this time. The mayor expressed his understanding of this problem and informed me that the military and civilian authorities are having regular meetings to put an end to such acts. He further regarded such a behaviour as a crime for which the perpetrators should be prosecuted." My question, Mr. Pasic, is: Can you explain to the Court what meetings you were referring to when you said that regular meetings were taking place between the military and civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just not sure that that question reflects what's in the memo which talks about civilian and military authorities are having regular meetings, not necessarily between themselves, and I just think the question might be a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think Ms. Gustafson is right, that the text does not give that detail, but we perhaps could inquire with the witness what he meant here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I disagree with that interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's ask him. Then we don't have to rely anymore on our interpretation but what the witness can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, it says that military and civilian authorities are having regular meetings to put an end to such acts. What meetings are you referring to, or were you referring to, when you had this discussion with Mr. Al-Alfi?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the meetings between General Cermak and the commissioners of the Government of Croatia, with the other participants, and they were the utilities company, the centre for social welfare, the Croatian Red Cross, and my associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And were you present at such meetings? And I mean specifically at meetings held to "put an end to such acts"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what steps you know of that were taken to "put to end to such acts," or were being discussed to put an end to such acts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: We asked that in places where -- in places liberated after Operation Storm that, at the check-points there, control be stepped up, entrance and exits, and the in-flow of people coming into Knin or leaving Knin. So basically control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This meeting was on the 18th of August, and I'd like to turn your attention to Exhibit P988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, Mr. Misetic, could I seek one clarification. You were asked about meetings the military and civilian authorities were engaged in. When asked with which authorities you referred to, you said -- which meetings you were referring to, you said Mr. Cermak meeting with, et cetera, et cetera. When talking about military authority, were you exclusively pointing at Mr. Cermak, or were there any other military authorities involved in talks on these matters; that is, to end such acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The other officers or persons in authority did not attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, Mr. President, it's P988, and I'm interested in page 7 of the English. But if we could first show the cover page so the witness is aware of what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report, Mr. Pasic, of the International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights about a fact-finding mission it conducted between 17th and 19th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to page 7 of this report. This is paragraph 5.1. I'm sorry, the next page, please. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the Helsinki Federation met with you as well on the same date as your meeting with Mr. Al-Alfi, on the 18th of August, 1995. And there the Helsinki Federation records the results of your conversation with the Helsinki Federation as follows: "We asked Pasic questions concerning the burnings and lootings. He replied with evasive and contradictory statements. He said that most of the destruction taking place is being carried out by civilians taking revenge. However, he did not elaborate or explain how he had come to that conclusion. We asked what measures he was taking to stop these civilians taking revenge, and he answered, I can do nothing, should we shoot them or what? Pasic also claimed" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Pasic also claimed that the 4th and 7th professional HV Brigades were not involved in any burning or looting but that individuals from the 6th Reserve Brigade were responsible." The next paragraph says: "When we asked Pasic about the man beaten at his apartment by HV soldiers and the elderly woman robbed by HV soldiers, he replied, I cannot guarantee anybody's safety." And then the next statements attributed to you are: "I do not apologise for what has happened here. "I could not prevent this from happening. "The position of the Croatian Government is that these people should say. "They need Croatian citizenship to come back." Now, first, let me ask you as a preliminary matter, do you recall meeting the Helsinki Federation on the 18th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that there were those representatives. I knew -- I know that one of the representatives wrote a column in Drago Pilsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall Petar Mrkalj being present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: The name doesn't ring a bell. It -- perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would it refresh your recollection if I told you that Mr. Mrkalj was the president of the Croatian Helsinki Committee at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the conversation or having a conversation with the Helsinki Federation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, they record you as giving evasive and contradictory statements. Do you wish to respond as to whether you were being evasive and contradictory at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has said he doesn't remember having this conversation. I'm not sure there is a basis for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is cross-examination. I'm entitled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if I say, I have no recollection of a meeting with Mr. A or B, then to ask where it took place, et cetera, of course, doesn't make much sense. It is about reporting. Of course, we could ask the witness whether he remembers that he ever, in any conversation, has been evasive, but if he has no specific recollection on this conversation, it's -- I do not see how he would have any knowledge which would allow him to -- to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to comment perhaps in a more general way that's appropriate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I will ask him more generally then, but I'm going to put it to him:

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, do you recall having any reason at the time to be evasive terms of what you were representing to the public as to what was taking place in Sector South at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No, there was no reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to come back for one second to the exchange, apparently Ms. Gustafson understood at the time, being during the meeting; whereas, you may have referred to at the time as a period. And that perhaps explains the exchange the views on this matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, although you don't recall the specifics of this meeting, was it your view on or around the 18th of August, or in that time-period, that the 4th and 7th professional HV Brigades were not involved in any burning or looting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain of that, because I toured the settlements around Knin, and it was said that this was not done by the members of the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, did they tell that you it was the 6th Reserve Brigade, the 6th Home Guard Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: As for the 6th Reserve or Home Guard Brigade, I hadn't heard of it. As far as I was concerned, there were only the 4th and the 7th Brigades. And there were a number of regiments, Home Guard Regiments, which took part in this operation, but I've never heard of this 6th Reserve Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you, Mr. Pasic, Exhibit P2319. This is an interview purportedly conducted with Petar Mrkalj and apparently involving Drago Pilsel in terms of how the interview was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 in the English. This is page 1 in the Croatian, and it's the middle column, the third column. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a question posed to Mr. Mrkalj who claims to have been with the Helsinki Federation fact-finding mission. He says -- he asked: What information did you obtain from the representatives of the Croatian authorities? Do you see that on the page, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. It says: "Mr. Petar Pasic told us that these were isolated cases and that he did not have detailed information. He also said that the houses were torched under somewhat emotional pressure. And finally he said that the Serb houses were not torched by the professional but Home Guard units of the Croatian Army. The head of the defence office in Knin told us the same thing, saying that there were four or five suspects and that there was no hard evidence for their arrest or for initiating any proceedings against them." Now, I know you don't recall the specifics of this meeting, Mr. Pasic, but if in fact you had had information that these houses -- first let me ask you this question. Was it your view at the time that these burnings were isolated cases, or was it a widespread phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: They were isolated cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And why do you say they were isolated cases?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Because, at the same time, nothing else was happening in a village. Well, there would be one house burning, and then perhaps in another settlement, there would be one or two houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You were the government's commissioner for Kistanje as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The Chamber has had -- heard evidence of burnings that took place in Kistanje, speaking now up to the date of the 18th August, which is when you had these meetings with the Helsinki Federation. Were you aware as the government's commissioner that there had been burnings in Kistanje, up to that point?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Up to that point, I don't think there was any large-scale burning in Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When did large-scale burning in Kistanje take place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I would have to say something before that, with your permission, and to explain something. Most of the people from Kistanje worked in the Sibenik area, and they worked at the metal factory there, for the aluminum industry. It was the TLM, Sibenska, Slobodna Plovidba, and the port of Sibenik. Unfortunately, immediately after the first barricades that were set up, they were set up between Sibenik and Kistanje at a place called Plancnik [phoen]. And it was at those barricades that those same people were seen who otherwise worked in the locations I mentioned earlier on, in the various factories. And when I said -- well, there's a term that I like to use, mental revenge, or retaliation and then what probably happened was, that the people that they worked with, when they were forced out of their homes and expelled, and when five or six years later they went back to their homes and found that their houses no longer existed but that trees were growing, fig trees or whatever, out of their yards and houses, they couldn't resist burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate the answer, Mr. Pasic, but my question, though, is you have said that up until the 18th, there wasn't large-scale burning in Kistanje. And my question is: When did the large-scale in Kistanje start, from your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: If there wasn't any until the 18th, probably it was later, but I cannot tell you when it took place or how long it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pasic, I'm going to suggest to that you if you're the government commissioner in Kistanje for that area, you probably have a general understanding of when a significant number of houses was burned down in an area where you are the government commissioner. And I will put to you that the Chamber has received evidence from a report of the United Nations Military Observers that roughly 150, approximately, houses out of approximately 500 houses in the Kistanje municipality were burned, and my question to you is: Can you tell the Chamber when the majority of that -- those 150 houses were burned? I know you said after the 18th, but do you have any more specific information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Let me first tell that I, indeed, was the commissioner for Kistanje, but I must also say that I was a government commissioner for four more municipalities, namely, Civljane, Biskupija, Ervenik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you please focus your answer on the question that was put to you. Mr. Misetic was not asking whether you had other functions. Mr. Misetic asked you when, what was reported as large-scale burning, when, according to your knowledge, that took place. If you know tell us; if you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of your earlier answers was that you don't think that there was any large-scale burning in Kistanje before the 18th. What made you think that there wasn't any large-scale burning in Kistanje before the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because those were the reports that were received from the people. Down there at Kistanje, there was a police station, and they received reports about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- well, apart from a police station being there, receiving reports from the ground, I think that people manning a police station would see by themselves whether there was any large-scale burning and that they would not be dependant on others reporting to them. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, later on, you said, If there wasn't any until the 18th, and you were referring to large-scale burning, you said, Probably it was later. Now, first of all, do you acknowledge that there was large-scale burning in Kistanje at any time in August/September 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you receive reports about it, or when did you observe yourself this to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was going to Sibenik, because I lived there, and passed -- in passing through Kistanje, I saw large-scale burning along the main road. It may have been around the 20th or the 25th of August of -- because it was then that I used to take that route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And earlier you did not take that route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I used to go through Drnis and Kosovo when I went to Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you say on the 20th and 25th, did you see large-scale burning, houses still in flames, or did you see the result of large-scale burning? That is, houses burned? What did you see, 20 or -- around the 20th or 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only saw the results. I didn't see flames or smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if it would have been around the 20th, would you then agree with me that it could well have been that the large-scale burning took place more than two days before that date; that is, before the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand from your testimony that you saw the results of large-scale burning on either the 20th -- around the 20th, or the 25th. Now -- and you also told us that what you saw is just the result, not the burning itself or houses in flames. Now, how could you conclude that there was no large-scale burning at the 18th or before the 18th, on the basis of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I travelled on several occasions from Knin through Kistanje to Sibenik, but I cannot say exactly whether it was on the 25th, whether it was in August, or at all, or in September, but I knew that when I travelled along that road, there was no large-scale burning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you -- did you ever receive reports about large-scale burning in Kistanje? Do you have any recollection of receiving reports about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you didn't see it, apart from that you saw the results which may have been either in August or in September; and you didn't ever receive any reports about that. That's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, while we're generally on this topic, you are aware, and forgive me if it's in your statement and I have not seen it, that the chief of the police of Kotar-Knin Cedo Romanic was, himself, an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: There are three -- three high officials in the town of Knin after Storm who were ethnic Serbs. There was me, there was Cedo Romanic as the chief of police, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A third person, whose name the interpreter didn't get.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I knew that they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay, the third person, the interpreter didn't get the name, but I think I heard you say Mr. Mihic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Milos Mihic, the chief of police at the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And obviously from your statements you had a good working relationship, according to you, with General Cermak as well. And my question to you is: If you can tell the Chamber or tell me if you had in fact seen crime, would there have been a reason for you not no report that crime to Mr. Romanic, to Mr. Mihic, if it involved civilian matters, or --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No, there couldn't have been reason for me not to report that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did -- again, let me ask you directly. You personally, as an ethnic Serb in the area, did you feel constrained from openly discussing criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me call up just so you -- so you have some familiarity with the document. As it document that's been admitted into evidence this morning, this is Exhibit D1714. And this relates to the issue of stolen grapes and corn. And this is page -- you discuss this at page 7 of your 2002 interview, which is -- it's D1706. And at page 7 -- I'm sorry. Actually, I don't know if it's at page 7. Page 5; I apologise. You say that this letter is a letter you sent to the police administration in Zadar and the police station in Knin, complaining that people were stealing grapes and corn, and nobody was stopping them. These people I listed by name in the letter and they wore -- and they were in both civilian and military clothing. As far as I know, nothing was done about it, because the stealing continued."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page to see the names as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this document is dated the 25th of October, 1995. And I wish to draw your attention to some observations of crime that appear in your 2002 statement. For example, at page 7 of your statement in English, you talk about going with Mr. Cermak's deputy, Marko Gojevic, to a village called Oton Bender. And you saw two Croatian soldiers with a tractor and trailer taking cattle away. Gojevic asked the soldiers why they were taking the cattle, and they replied that they were recovering what they had lost. Also on page 7 you talk about an incident of seeing Croatian soldiers collecting horses and putting them on trucks and taking them away. And then, I believe, there was the incident of -- which you have corrected in your supplemental information sheet, about travelling from Sibenik to Knin and always stopped in Drnis at a check-point where you see what you have now corrected as civilians driving trucks full of goods. My question is: With respect do each of these incidents, did you file a report with the Knin police station or the police administration in Zadar for -- where you observed goods being stolen, items being looted, cattle and horses being taken, et cetera, did you file similar reports for those observations as you did for -- with specific names of people stealing grapes and corn, which you filed on the 25th of October?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: This report about the theft of grapes and corn wasn't drafted by me. There was an office of the ministry of agriculture and forestry in Knin with two staff. They submitted a list of those who were caught stealing grapes and corn, and I simply forwarded their letter to the police administration in Zadar and the police station at Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, your testimony -- the witness statement indicates that some of these people on this list are persons either in the Croatian military or wearing military uniforms. I presume, and you correct me if I'm wrong, that the majority of these people, if not all of them, are ethnic Croats. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, don't hold this against me, but I really couldn't tell, whether they were ethnic Serbs or ethnic Croats by the way they were dressed. And if I may amend, judging by the place of residence of these people and by their first and last names, if I may, I would conclude that most of them were ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My point is that, on the 25th of October, you did not have a problem signing your name to a document which was reporting to the police theft by ethnic Croats. Am I right? You weren't afraid to do this. Or were you afraid?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So to go back to my question, I understand that this report may have been prepared by someone else. But if you, for example, saw horses being stolen or cattle being stolen, given the fact that you worked with Mr. Mihic and Mr. Romanic and General Cermak, would there have been a reason why you wouldn't have reported that -- or let me ask the first question. Did you report -- the incidents that you've described in your statement, did you report them to Mr. Mihic or Mr. Romanic or anyone else in the police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: All the incidents that happened in the field I pointed out to Mr. Romanic and Mr. Mihic orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would they take action? Do you know if they would take action, if you reported these types of incidents to them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: The later chief of police of Knin, because the Kotar was done away with, and Mr. Mihic returned to Sibenik, so the chief of police at Knin became Mr. Viroza [phoen] and I reported some events to him, some incidents. And he said to me that he -- he submitted written reports to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could we seek clarification of the answer. One of your previous answers was all the incidents that happened in the field I pointed out to Mr. Romanic and Mr. Mihic orally. Then you were asked whether they took any action upon your report. And then you come with a story that someone else was, at a later stage, police chief, and that -- but the question put to you by Mr. Misetic simply was where you said you reported to Mr. Romanic and Mr. Mihic, whether they took any action. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that, due to their place in the hierarchy, it was their duty to inform their superiors in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was whether they took any action, not whether they were duty-bound to do so. Do you know that, or don't you know it? If you don't know, tell us; if you do know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that they took any action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You don't think they took any action which now leads to the question as to why they didn't take any action. Mr. Romanic specifically was someone who you would attend the meetings -- with whom you would attend meetings at General Cermak's office on a daily or almost daily basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Romanic ever explain why he wasn't taking any action on matters that you personally had reported to him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him or follow up with him to say, Whatever happened with the stolen cattle or stolen horses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
