utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to page 7 of D1706, which is the 2002 statement. And there you talk about -- let me find the Croatian page for you. Here we go, it's page 11 in the B/C/S. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the bottom, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You say: "I also went to the Plavno village and saw Croatian soldiers collecting horses and putting them on trucks and taking them away. I am aware of a woman called Marta Vujanovic being killed and she came from Oton Polje. She was killed with her mentally-retard son. There are three hamlets in Oton, Oton Bender, Oton Brdo, and Oton Polje. I heard that this woman was killed from my uncle, Luka Pasic." And I'd like to turn your attention on this incident, Mr. Pasic, to Exhibit P2345, at English page 62 and B/C/S page 60, please. Mr. Pasic, what we're going to see on it's screen is a report by the Croatian Helsinki Committee. It was published in Croatian in 1999, and the English version was published in 2001. And you can see in the Croatian version the paragraph in the middle of your screen there, that begins: "At the end of August 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is at the bottom of the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me read it out to you. It says: "At the end of August 1995" -- I'm sorry. Let me start with the paragraph preceding, so we understand the context. It says: "The other example of a similar search ended up tragically. A day after military Operation Storm ended, a daughter of Marta Vujanovic, born in 1905, who lives in Germany asked about her mother born in 1905 and brother's, Stevo, destiny born in 1939. She knew that Marta and Stevo remained in the village of Oton, but the Knin authorities refused to help her. "At the end of August 1995 she wrote a letter to the Croatian Helsinki Committee asking for help. The CHC office demanded that the commissioner of the government, Petar Pasic, help them. Mr. Pasic did not reply to any of the written demands on behalf of the CHC. However, he showed a letter to the international observers and said, I have more important job to do than look around Knin and collect Serb corpses. When he had said that, Marta Vujnovic and her son had already been dead. The Croatian soldiers killed them on August 18th, 1995, in their own house, Mother Marija, was killed inside the house, and Stevo in his own yard. If Petar Pasic had listened to her daughter and sister Lubica, it would be possible that they would be alive today together with other residents of Oton killed that same day." Now my first question, Mr. Pasic, is, do you remember any of this -- did it in fact happen that there was correspondence between you and the Croatian Helsinki Committee with the daughter of Marta Vujnovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Based on this, I cannot confirm that what is said here is true. Because, at the time, there was -- there were no telephone lines, functioning telephone lines between Knin and other towns which can be easily verified. I personally knew the killed -- that killed person. We are even related. So if I had known about that, I certainly would have helped. But it's impossible that she spoke to me over the phone, because there were no functioning phone lines at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I read the Serbian news -- or, rather, the news in the Serbian newspapers, but I'm not sure what identity this was, because they talk about this story in a different way. And mostly in the article that I read it did not refer to Petar Pasic but the problems which occurred in Donji Lapac, Benkovac, Gracac, and some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian Helsinki Committee claims that there was correspondence between you -- I'm sorry, from them to you, meaning from the Helsinki -- Croatian Helsinki Committee, that there were written demands sent to you by them. Do you recall such written demands?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: All there is, is one written request, as far as I remember, from the Helsinki Committee sent to me and that was when a convoy from a barracks when on its way to Serbia, and I remember this, the number was 619. That was its number. And there was a person there called Stana Grkinjic [phoen]. And along the way en route somewhere, she disappeared. And her daughter informed both me and the Helsinki Committee and then -- well, it was Mr. Cicak at the time who was the president of the HHO, and he simply wrote a letter to me. He said, Mr. Commissioner, please look for that person and try and find her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm interested also in knowing how the name of Marta Vujnovic wound up in your 2002 statement. Were you aware at the time of the 2002 statement of the allegations that had been made against you by the HHO in its reports of 1999 and 2002, concerning Marta Vujnovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it happened to be there in the first place because the village of Plavno, when we talk about horses and so on, this is quite a different matter -- or Konji [phoen], and there are two settlements at a distance of 15 to 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know if Mr. Foster and Mr. Casey, the Prosecution's investigators, showed you the HHO, the Croatian Helsinki Committee report, at the time of the interview that you gave them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, you don't know; or, no, they didn't show it to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say no, they did not show you the report. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I think that's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Pasic, let me switch to a different subject. This is Exhibit P822. This is a report from an ECMM monitor. Do you recall a man named Soren Liborius of the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if we look at this report, if we look towards the bottom of the first paragraph, it says -- he describes a meeting that he held -- I'm sorry, a meeting with Mr. Gambotti, between you and Mr. Gambotti. Do you remember Mr. Gambotti?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of that paragraph it says: "Returning Serbs, according to Mr. Pasic more than 100 have reported from Serbia, the number growing every day." And then there's a comment: "Indeed some people are returning but only those with property secured. The team still wait to see when an actual occupant of a house is driven out because the legal owner returned." And the date is the 27th of October of this report. My question -- I had asked you earlier at the beginning of my questioning, Mr. Pasic, about the number of returned Serbs as of April 1996. Do you recall the accuracy of this report, that 100 Serbs had returned from Serbia by the end of October 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Neither me nor my office were in a position to keep statistical data about the number of those who returned, but what I said was those who did return and came to us, many of them returned but didn't come to see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so is it your testimony or was it your report on that day that 100 Serbs had returned from Serbia and had come to you, seeking help, but there could have been more?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where would you -- where would these Serbs, these 100 Serbs who had came back that you knew of, where would they be housed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Usually -- well, since the flats and houses in Knin were already occupied most of the people who returned went back to villages around Knin in actual fact because they were from those parts in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would they go back to their own homes, or would you put them up in other peoples' homes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No. They would see to their own accommodation, and we did write a letter and tried to put some people up in a centre, in Strmica, but all those people refused and declined collective accommodation and went back to their native villages, because most of them did have family homes in the villages but were allotted flats, socially-owned flats, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, are you saying Serbs who came back were also allotted flats, socially-owned flats, in Knin in addition to their own homes that they had in the outlying villages?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, who is it that was allotted socially-owned flats in Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, attached to the Government of Croatia, there was a commission for accommodation, and at the request of individuals they would allot flats for temporary use, temporary accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Why -- you mentioned you tried to put some people up in a centre in Strmica. Why were you trying to put people up in a centre in Strmica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, until their homes were refurbished we wanted to provide them with temporary accommodation and our people, and I'm from the area, were such that they refused to go into collective accommodation. They didn't want to do that, so they preferred to live in houses that were partially destroyed and been burnt. But with the help of international organisations, they did meet the necessary conditions -- well, they were given the necessary conditions to be able to live in these houses until they were reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You first said that most of the them did have family homes in the villages but were allotted flats, socially-owned flats, in Knin. Mr. Misetic asked you whether, in addition to the homes they had, that flats were allotted. And the answer was no. I have difficulties in understanding exactly the relation between flats being given to people returning, where you said it was not in addition to their own homes, even if partly destroyed. Who then got these flats or apartments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you understood me. The flats, well, after returning from Serbia, these people were not allotted flats. What I said was that they returned -- that they were given these flats, allotted these flats before Operation Storm. But as families, they lived in the villages. So they were able to go back to the houses that had either been devastated or those that could still be used for living. So the returnees, or at least many of them, were not allotted the flats that they had used before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let me try to verify whether I understood you well. Those who had been living in flats, socially-owned flats, in Knin, after they returned from Serbia, they preferred not to return to their socially-owned flats, but, rather would go to their family homes, destroyed or partly destroyed, in the villages where they originated from. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not quite. Let me explain. The -- by decision of the government of Croatia, the flats had been allocated to other users now. So the Serbs who were returning could not go back, did not go back to their former flats or to any other flats for that matter. In their desire to return, they returned to their family homes, family houses from which they -- which they left when they were allotted these flats previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when these flats were allotted to them and, as you told us, later being allotted to other people, would that include Croatian citizens from Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain that question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I would like to know, whether those who had been living in those flats and apartments in Knin and upon return from Serbia could not use them anymore, would there among them, people as well, who were Croatian citizens but of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of those people who left, and you know that the problem the accommodation is still being resolved today, nobody returned to their flats, whether they were Serbs or Croats, those who left for Serbia after Operation Storm or went to Bosnia after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And upon return, they couldn't use the flats they previously had occupied in accordance with the normal regulations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither the flats, nor any other premises, nor anything else, furniture or whatever. They couldn't use that anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why couldn't they use their furniture anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, pursuant to a decision taken by the Government of Croatia and the housing commission, that housing space was given to other people who had come into Knin after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that included the furniture, and if someone would come back and say, Well, this is my couch, or my fridge or my bed, what would be the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, many people didn't even dare do that, knock on the door of their former flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why wouldn't they dare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was another tenant there, another occupant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But still their furniture. They had paid for their beds, I take it, and for their fridges and for their tables and chairs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By decision of the government, well, we had social ownership of property previously. Now there was no socially-owned property anymore. I had a flat in Sibenik, for example, and I could buy it up, I could purchase it myself, whereas these other flats had not been purchased. There was no longer any socially-owned accommodation. So it was only a question of furniture and things like that, whether somebody was willing to cede the furniture or not. There were cases like that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to understand. You said these people left their flats they had occupied, which were socially-owned flats or apartments. Now you say upon their return, they found these flats to be occupied. But are you telling that it was not socially-owned anymore? Then, if not, who had ownership of those flats previously occupied by this Serb family, which wished to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every flat or the flat of every employer. Let's assume he worked for the Croatian railways, for example, a worker of the Croatian railways or something else, those flats belonged to the Croatian railways. Now, if it was a flat belonging to the utilities company, everybody working in the utilities company would be allocated a flat to live in by the company, and so these flats belonged to the various enterprises. And somebody taking occupancy, taking up occupancy later on would get a certificate saying that he had temporary use of the flat, so it didn't belong to him. The flat still belonged to the ministry in which the person worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's clear to me that is it was later allotted to other persons; it may not have been the ownership of the company anymore, but it was the government who decided who would occupy that flat. Now I get back to the furniture. The furniture was not socially-owned? The furniture was still owned by those who had previously lived in that flat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said people would not dare to go there and claim their own furniture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you assist them in re-gaining their furniture, or would you just accept that those who were now occupying the flats would use the fridges, the beds, the tables, the chairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We accepted the existing situation. Unfortunately, I have to say, that I, too, was allocated a flat for temporary accommodation, but that the person who lived there before me never turned up, he never asked for his furniture back or his flat back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you describe a situation, and we're talking about an attitude towards those who left, that it was wished - that's at least part of the evidence this Chamber has heard - that people were encouraged to return. Now, could you reconcile the fact that if you would return, that you would have no furniture anymore. Your flat would be occupied by others. What was the attractive perspective that was offered to those who wished to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that everybody actually wanted to return. There was that wish. And every person hoped that, if they returned, for example, the village I came from, that, ultimately, they would have the opportunity of going back to their flat at some point. But let me explain. Every person who left and, pursuant to Croatian government decision, did not return within six months or did not send in a request to have their flat returned to them, were not able to do so. And it's only now that these requests are being dealt with. So those who tabled their requests in 1998 or 1999, those cases are still pending. But flats and houses were not an obstacle to people who wanted to come back to their origins and native area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic. I'm also looking at the clock. I don't know whether this would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I was going to turn to a new topic, so it might be a good time for a break then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break, and we will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could you keep in mind that I would like to reserve some seven or eight minutes at the end of this meeting for procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I anticipate I will be done well before the end so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Ms. Gustafson, would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, first a correction to the record, I put to the witness Exhibit P2345 which is, I have been now told, MNA status, and what I should have called out is P2402, which is in evidence, but it is a redacted version of P2345, and so the record should be clear. The pages, however, are the same in both documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's now clearly on the record, Mr. Misetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to shift gears here for one minute and ask you a few questions concerning the statement you made on the 2nd of August. This is discussed at paragraph 10 of your 2009 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to that. It's D1707.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you're referring to -- back to your 2002 statement, which is D1706, at paragraph 10, and you were asked by the Cermak Defence what did you mean when you said you were -- by the term "trouble to come." And you explained that you believed that the plights of the civilian population would be repeated like in the previous HV operations Maslenica, Medacki Dzep, and Bljesak, particularly since Knin town was the epicentre of and synonymous with the rebellion against the Republic of Croatia constitutional order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is if you could please clarify what you were referring to concerning the plight of the civilian population repeated, like in those operations.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: As I have said before, I'm a citizen of the Republic of Croatia of Serb ethnicity. Since 1991, I have been in the focus of events, and after each operation of the Croatian Army, and there have been several, I can mention Miljevci, then came Maslenica, then there was the Dubrovnik coast-line, Sinj and the surroundings, the Medak pocket, Flash. In each of these operations the civilian population suffered most. That is, the population that lived in these areas. I expected something of that kind to happen at Knin, because Knin was the epicentre of the rebellion against the illegally-elected Croatian Government, and that's why the plights there could even exceed those in the earlier operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, what is it that you expected would happen specifically when you talk about the plight?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I expected an exodus to occur; and it, indeed, happened. The civilian population left in organised convoys, which a so-called army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina did to its own population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what was the basis of this expectation? Why did you expect that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I expected that because the previous operations resulted in the civilian population suffering most badly, and they mostly left the areas that were put under the control of the Croatian authorities or the Croatian police, even -- even though it was possible to remain in those areas, and yet many people left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, did you expect that the -- when you said this on the 2nd of August, were you expecting that if Croatia took over control of Knin town, that Croatia or its organs would treat the civilian population badly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to show you the video-clip of the Croatian TV newscast on the 2nd of August which carried your call to the Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this will be 65 ter 1D2980.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Sasa Kopljar: ...the Croatian government commissioner for Knin, Petar Pasic, sent an open letter to the citizens of Serb nationality in Knin who, according to Pasic, in the last couple of days have been unable to leave the town because of the barriers placed at every entrance to the town in order to prevent them from escaping from an already apparent disarray. Your time is nearly up, but it may not be too late to turn your backs on your steeped-in-crime leaders who are leading you to suffering and hell, wrote Pasic, calling the citizens of Knin to accept the peaceful hand of negotiations of Croatia in Geneva, and to renounce their dissident authorities and acknowledge the Republic of Croatia as their sole homeland. At the same time, the self-proclaimed Serb authorities are continuing with their intensive ethnic cleansing of the area of north-western Bosnia. Another 119 refugees of Croatian nationality from the wider Banja Luka area, mostly from the village of Simic, fled by boats from Srbac across the Sava River to Drvar on the Croatian coast."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, is that in fact the -- how your letter was transmitted over Croatian state television to those in the so-called Krajina who could watch Croatian television?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Other than this report on Croatian television, were there other means through which your letter was broadcast or disseminated to the Krajina Serb population?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: According to the information available to me, not such a letter, but there was a comment on the TV channel of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina in which that letter was called a threat to the Serb population in the area of the so-called RSK, and in a very ugly manner, they spoke both about the Croatian state and the commissioner of the Croatian government, calling him an Ustasha commissioner or Tudjman's brown-nose. And in the so-called RSK, especially in the media, the term member of the Croatian people was rarely used. Instead, they used a phrase part of the Ustasha people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D2980 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1716.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1716 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to seek a clarification to page 6 of your 2002 statement, which is, again, D1706. In it, you state that General Gotovina's headquarters had moved from Split to Knin and was housed next door to Cermak's office. Are you aware that, in fact, General Gotovina's headquarters at all times in 1995, the headquarters itself, was in Split and remained in Split but that there was forward command post that had also been set up in Knin.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I know the term "command post" and "forward command post," but I don't know, really. I suppose that the garrison of General Gotovina was in Split and that the forward command post was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I take it from your answer you mean that -- you suppose that the command of General Gotovina was in Split, but the forward command post was in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if it just a supposition, do we need a clarification of what is supposed? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Pasic, if you had felt -- let -- this question arises from the 2002 statement, much of which you have clarified now, but I wanted to ask you this question anyway. If you felt that you were a figurehead with no real authority, and if you felt -- if had you felt that there was some sort of a policy to allow crime to take place, would you have stayed in that position as the commissioner of the Knin region?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the question is highly hypothetical and calls for speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but even if it is a hypothesis, then that doesn't mean that it's speculation because the witness is asked about what he would do, and that could be something that he has formed an opinion about already, and, under those circumstances, it would not be speculation, but, rather, thoughts about what to do under what circumstances. Therefore, the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Croatian Government trusted me in my work, because if it hadn't been the case, I wouldn't have stayed in the position of commissioner from the 5th of August till the 9th of March, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. My question, though, is specifically asking you about your perspective on things and my question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, perhaps, also in view of my ruling on your last issue -- Did you give it ever any thought, Mr. Pasic, that you could have been used as a figurehead with no real authority? Did it ever come to your mind as a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever think about that, if this would be the case, how you would react, or have you not even thought about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I partly thought about that. If it had been the case, it would have been difficult for me to accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- well, sometimes it may be difficult to accept, but what would you have done? Would have you stayed, or would you have quit? What -- in what would this difficult acceptance have resulted, in your thoughts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my thoughts, or, rather, I didn't think along the lines of making a living. It was about the majority of expelled Croats and Serbs having confidence in me. Some didn't, but they were a minority, and they held opposed -- their position was opposed to mine. I must say that the situation in Knin, in spite of all the efforts made by the garrison and the commissioner and the government of the Republic of Croatia, didn't develop the way it should have. I said that on March the 9th I was replaced, and I became commissioner of the Croatian Government for four other municipalities. My deputy, that is the man who replaced me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are moving away from the question, Mr. Pasic. I asked you whether you had considered for this possibility. You said you partly thought about that and that, if that would be the case, that it would have been difficult to accept that. Would the difficulty of accepting it, would that have had any consequences in what you would have done, in your thoughts? Would you have said, I would have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it wouldn't have changed your behaviour. Is that how I am to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I tried to avoid hypothesis and to get it in a clear context, as you may have been aware of. To some extent, it is the phrasing of the question which is also of importance to whether we are not -- we are asking the witness to speculate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. If have you any follow-up questions, I have got no problems with that, let me be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I do. It's just -- again, it's a little bit of a difficulty of the 2002 statement, so I'm assuming that my colleagues across the well are going to state that those -- that statement has -- was accurate. And if that is the case, then my question, and I will try to be more specific on it, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if you felt when you were in Knin, in August and September of 1995, that burning and looting was something that had been approved or planned from above, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: If it had been planned and implemented like that, I wouldn't have agreed to be part of that system and part of those authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Gustafson. Ms. Gustafson is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to begin by asking you some questions about your various statements and your subsequent corrections. And you first gave a statement to the Prosecution - that was back in 2001 and 2002 - and you don't need to look at it at the moment, if you could just listen to my question. Because it's not actually related to the contents of that. Now, at that time, the statement was prepared in English and the interpreter sat down with you and read it back to you in Croatian. Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And after the interpreter read it back to you, it was then that you signed the statement and initialled each page of it, on the English version; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I can complete this. I gave my statement on two occasions. On the first two days when I gave my statement, it wasn't read to me, either in English or Croatian. Only in March of the following year, 2002, that statement was read in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. And it was read to you in March of 2002, and after it was read to you, that's when you signed it and initialled every page; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I think so, but ... I'm not sure whether I initialled every page or simply put my signature at the end of the document, the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it's in evidence, Mr. Pasic, you can take it from me that your initials are on every page. And now you gave your second statement to the Defence, the Cermak Defence, than was -- that took place on 22nd of November 2007 and the 18th of February, 2009. And today in your testimony and as well written in that statement, you confirmed that when you gave your statement to the Defence, you read your Prosecution statement, and I'd like to ask you, at that time were you actually given a hard copy of your Prosecution statement in Croatian to read over?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you read it over, both on the 22nd of November of 2007, and, again, on the 18th of February, 2009; or was it just on one of those occasions that you read over your Prosecution statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Initially, I only read the statement very superficially. I didn't appreciate its full significance, because I thought that that statement would never be used, although it says there the International Criminal Tribunal, and I signed at a time when I may have been a bit too confused. So I didn't attach so much significance to it. But I'm the only one to blame for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like you to answer my question, which is: Did you read your Prosecution statement both on the 22nd of November, 2007, when you met with the Cermak Defence and on the 18th of February, 2009, when you met with them again; or did you only read it over on one of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I read it several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you read it both on the 22nd of November and -- in 2007, and on the 18th of February 2009. Is that -- do I correctly understand you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were you given -- did the Cermak Defence, at that time, when they took that second statement from you, did they actually give you a copy of your Prosecution statement in Croatian to keep?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And we've heard today that you recently met again with the Cermak Defence on the 2nd of September, 2009, a few weeks ago. And at that meeting, the -- the note of that meeting says that: "The purpose of the meeting was to confirm his statement for the Rule 92 ter procedure." So my question is: At that time in September 2009 when you met with the Cermak Defence, I take it they asked to you read over both of your previous statements again. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: What I said was that I wasn't cautious enough in -- towards the statement that I gave. But I read both the statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it, at that time, the meeting on the 2nd of September, you were aware, they either made you aware then, or you were already aware that you would be called as a witness for the Cermak Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: It was only last Friday that I was informed by the Tribunal that I would be an official witness. Up until then, I still didn't know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When did the Cermak Defence first inform you that you would be a witness for the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I think that was before, when we met for the first time in Split. But official information, saying that I was a potential candidate for -- or, rather, I was a candidate as a witness for the Cermak Defence case, but official information I received on the 2nd or 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So the Cermak Defence first informed you that may be a witness for the Cermak Defence when you gave them your statement back in 2007 and 2009, and then they confirmed that you were definitely a witness when you met with them on the 2nd of September, 2009. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: It didn't confirm that. It wasn't the Cermak counsel who confirmed that. It was confirmed by the Registry of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pasic, the note of the meeting that you had on the 2nd of September with the Cermak Defence says that the purpose was to confirm your statement for the Rule 92 ter procedure. So I take it then that they explained to you that they were planning to call you as a witness and that your statements would be given do the Trial Chamber as evidence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, most probably they intended to call me. But let me repeat, I was officially informed that I would be coming in as a witness from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there seems to be quite some confusion. I do understand that last Friday, you got a message from the Registry that you would go to The Hague in order to testify. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, early September of this year, five weeks ago, you were interviewed by the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they tell you that they intended to examine you as a witness before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did they tell you that they intended to tender your witness statements, to give them to the Trial Chamber as your evidence in this case? Did they tell you that on the 2nd of September?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on that occasion, on the 2nd of September, you made a number of corrections to your Prosecution statement. At the end of those corrections, you said: "Pasic informed the Defence that he thinks he did not pay sufficient attention when he read his statement." Now, I understand that statement to mean - and correct me if I'm wrong - that when you met with the Cermak Defence on the 2nd of September, you explained to them the reason why you had to make additional corrections to your Prosecution statement was the fact that, on previous occasions, you had not paid sufficient attention when you read your Prosecution statement. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, then, in light of that, I would think that you would have read your Prosecution and Defence statements over more carefully than you had previously on the 2nd of September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: All these additions to the statement, I proposed to the Cermak Defence team. None of them said -- none of them told me to write something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's not my question, Mr. Pasic. My question is: On the 2nd of September, having realised that you had not paid sufficient attention on previous occasions, you read your Prosecution statement over more carefully; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pasic, when did you arrive in The Hague? What day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I arrived in The Hague on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when did you first meet with the Cermak Defence, after you arrived in The Hague? Do you remember when you met with them first?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how was that meeting arranged? Who contacted whom to arrange that meeting on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when did you first inform the Cermak Defence that you wanted to make additional changes to your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: When I saw that I had made some omissions in previous -- my previous reading of the statements. I felt the need to make some additions to the statements and incorporate some elements that I had omitted earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when was that? When did you inform the Cermak Defence of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that was ... on the 1st or 2nd. Well, I don't know what the date was, but I know that we were -- that I suggested that these changes be made.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Pasic, my question wasn't clear. I meant after your -- the changes you made in September. After that, when did you first inform the Cermak Defence that you wanted to make additional changes, the changes that we -- that you made just the other day, just on Tuesday. When did you tell the Cermak Defence you wanted to make those changes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I -- when was that date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I think that Mr. Kay asked you to seek permission when you wanted to consult papers. The question simply is: This same week, when did you tell the Cermak Defence that there were additional changes you would like to make? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was the 2nd of September, that that was the slot -- or, rather, the 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is -- well, the 10th of October is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the 2nd of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2nd of October. And you said you arrived this Tuesday in The Hague? That's the day before yesterday. Yes, did you give them a phone call on the 2nd of October or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 2nd of October, I met with Mr. Zeljko Basic from the Defence team for General Gotovina. He was passing through, going from Split to Sibenik, and I asked to meet with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just if -- I'm sorry for counsel, but if the counsel could ask for clarification as to which team we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the transcript reads that you with Mr. Zeljko Basic from the Defence team for General Gotovina. Did you mean -- did you mean Cermak --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon, I meant Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you phoned him on the 2nd of October, and you said -- you said what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: I said that I had received information, telling me that I was going to be a witness, and I was told when and at what time. And then I saw that I was in a bit of a predicament since some statements that I had given to the Prosecutors in 2002 do not stand, since I changed a part with respect to General Cermak. I was supposed to change -- well, as far as I was concerned, as a commissioner of the Croatian government, these statements do not stand, as far as the events that happened after Operation Storm are concerned as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You phoned Mr. Basic on the 2nd of October. When did you receive the phone call from the Registry that you were officially going to be a witness in this trial?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: On Friday, the previous day. I was called up by a lady from the Registry of the Tribunal, Mrs. Or Ms. Lily.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And between the time that Ms. Or Mrs. Lily called you on Friday and the next day when you called Mr. Basic, between those two phone calls, did you read your Prosecution statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I'm a bit confused about the 2nd of October. You said the day after that. The witness said he received a phone call on Friday, which was the 2nd of October, and that he called Mr. Basic on the 2nd. So I have difficulties in understanding the day after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I hadn't done the counting. He had said on Friday the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I wonder if it might help if he could see a calendar or something like that, if that would meet with the Court's approval. It sometimes helps people to remember days of the week and dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, talking about time, Ms. Gustafson, I asked to you keep in mind as well that I would need seven minutes. We are now at a point where there are just seven minutes remaining. So I would suggest that we leave it for the time being. Mr. Pasic, we'll continue tomorrow, but I want to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, the testimony you gave today - and, of course, tomorrow there will still be testimony to be given - I would -- so you shouldn't speak with anyone, not on the phone, not in any other way, just don't talk about your testimony with anyone. And then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Pasic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three brief matters. First, when looking, and we dealt with that earlier, about the translation of the statement of the witness, I see that the B/C/S version reads, and forgive me for my pronunciation [B/C/S spoken], which I haven't checked it but looks very much as a kind of a working version of the translation. Usually we're informed what kind of translation we have in our hands. But apparently here we are dealing with a work document rather than a final translation. So could you please verify the status. Mr. Kay is tendering it, but it has been prepared apparently by -- I don't know by whom but at the request of the Prosecution. It is of some concern to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe it's a CLSS translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But nevertheless, it says that the B/C/S at the top, and it's not contradicted, so my understanding of the Croatian or B/C/S is growing. That meets some concern and it should be verified what the exact status of that translation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A schedule of the differences has been done by the Cermak Defence during the proceedings this morning, Your Honour. That -- I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have to further pay attention to that. We are not in a position at this moment. If you could share that with Prosecution and/or CLSS, that would certainly speed up resolution of this -- of this apparent problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's done, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Cermak Defence has filed, on the 2nd of October, six motions under Rule 92 bis, which results in some 1500 pages, approximately. It could be 1300 or 1700, I'm not -- the Chamber would -- before the Prosecution responds to this motion, the Chamber would further like to discuss with the parties how to proceed in relation to the subject matter covered by these 92 bis statements. Therefore, don't hurry, Mr. Waespi, to have your response already filed today and perhaps wait until the Chamber has given it some further thought on what would be the most efficient way of -- and receiving this evidence, and to work in such a way that we do not lose time on exercises which can -- without any prejudice for the Cermak Defence could be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're very conscious of that, you know that the Rule 68 disclosure on this matter has been an ongoing issue. Those documents come from the first steps taken by us. We have it very much in mind that this information should be scheduled and put in a digestible form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you already could give that some thought, then -- because the Chamber will think about it a while as how to digest a large number of pages. And you should be aware that if we receive 1500 pages, we'll read 1500 pages and analyse them in such detail as is required. So that, of course, triggers the further thinking of the Chamber on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've had discussions between the Prosecution and the Defence on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps we might further encourage -- if -- has this been --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's -- it's a matter -- it's the disclosure just dealing with it, we -- we have very much in mind the concerns the Court has. We were aware of it when we served it, but we had these materials and it was the best way to proceed with the first materials we had. But we're very conscious of the fact that those materials would be put into a schedule, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or to be presented in another way. As I said before, how the chamber will receive this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'm not denying any right of presenting evidence. But it's just the form in which it is presented and -- okay. We'll deal with that later, but Mr. Waespi knows that he doesn't have to make over-hours this evening to file a response. Then, as far as next week, Thursday, is concerned, the 15th of October, there are still considerable problems in scheduling the video-conference link on that day. I just want to inform the parties about that. In addition to that, I can already tell the parties that where I said that we have to apply Rule 15 bis anyhow for part of the day, that in addition to that, we would not have the full afternoon session available. Most likely not any further than until 6.00. That is also to be kept in mind. If this, in terms of time needed to elicit evidence from these two witnesses would trigger any further thoughts as to whether that would be enough, the Chamber would like to know. Otherwise, the Chamber will consider whether it's feasible at all to have this videolink next week, Thursday. We are still working on it, but it is just already a flag for the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I -- sorry, Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt. It's just on this distinct issue. It seems me this witness is going to go into tomorrow. The witness scheduled for tomorrow will go into Monday, and we have a witness already listed for Monday who will then continue, and then another witness. It may be to all intents and purposes better to draw a line under that now so that decisions are able to be made on the scheduling of the witnesses, se we have a clear plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to have then have these witnesses scheduled for either the end of October or the first days of November through videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're very much thinking along those lines and looking at the dates for the last batch of witnesses that are to be held after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll include that in our considerations, Mr. Kay. Then one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In order not to collide with the Chamber who is using this courtroom this afternoon, I refrain from -- what I had in mind is to read practical guidance on bar table submissions. We'll leave that for tomorrow. We adjourn. We will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 9th of October, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
